_meta.provenance_policy: Factual and judgment fields are Claude drafts until an author sets status to 'approved'. 'commentary' is author-only and is never drafted by Claude.
_meta.headline_policy: Each headline was checked against a Wayback Machine snapshot of the original page (the visible h1 where available; otherwise og:title or <title>). 'url' is the original; 'archive_url' is the snapshot to link to. Notes record any differences.

cases.title: Please Rob Me lists people who have left home

headlines.text: Please Rob Me Makes Foursquare Super Useful For Burglars
Please Rob Me and the problem with social media
Foursquare Responds To Please Rob Me: Please Shut Up

what_happened.text: A Dutch website scraped public Foursquare check-ins that users had auto-posted to Twitter and displayed them as a scrolling list of people who were not at home, filterable by city. Its creators said the aim was to warn people against broadcasting their whereabouts. The site also messaged each listed user on Twitter.

outcome_detail.text: Foursquare published a privacy post the next day. Check-in services continued to operate as before.

responses.summary: Published a blog post on privacy the following day.

cases.title: Street View cars collected Wi-Fi payload data

headlines.text: Google admits collecting Wi-Fi data through Street View cars
Google Admits Its Street View Cars Collected Personal Wi-Fi Data
Google Admits Accidentally Intercepting Users' Private Data With Street View Cars
headlines.note: Later admission (Oct 2010) that full emails and passwords were captured.

what_happened.text: After an audit requested by Germany's data protection authority, Google said its Street View cars had been recording fragments of 'payload' data (content such as emails and web pages) from unencrypted home Wi-Fi networks, in addition to network names and hardware addresses. Two weeks earlier, a Google blog post had said the company did not collect payload data. Google attributed the collection to experimental code written in 2006.

outcome_detail.text: The FCC fined Google $25,000 in 2012, for impeding its investigation rather than for the collection itself. In March 2013 Google paid $7 million to 38 states and DC and agreed to destroy the payload data.

responses.summary: Said it had been 'mistakenly collecting samples of payload data' from open Wi-Fi networks and grounded its Street View cars.

sources.label: The Register on the $7M settlement, 13 Mar 2013

cases.title: iPhones kept a hidden log of locations

headlines.text: iPhone keeps record of everywhere you go
Your iPhone Keeps a Secret Log of Everywhere You Go, Security Experts Find
Researchers: Apple's iPhone Keeps Track Of Every Little Place You Go

what_happened.text: Researchers Pete Warden and Alasdair Allan found a file, consolidated.db, on iPhones and 3G iPads running iOS 4 that stored timestamped latitude and longitude records, in some cases going back about a year, and that was copied to users' computers during backups. They found no evidence the data was sent to Apple.

outcome_detail.text: Apple said it was not tracking users and called the retention a bug. iOS 4.3.3, released about a week later, cut the cache to seven days, stopped backing it up, and deleted it when location services were off. A Senate Judiciary subcommittee held a hearing on 10 May 2011.

responses.summary: Statement of 27 April 2011: Apple is not tracking iPhone locations; the file is a cache of Wi-Fi hotspot and cell tower locations used to speed up positioning; the long retention was a bug.

sources.label: Macworld on Apple's congressional testimony, May 2011

cases.title: Girls Around Me maps women's check-ins with their Facebook profiles

headlines.text: This Creepy App Isn’t Just Stalking Women Without Their Knowledge, It’s A Wake-Up Call About Facebook Privacy
headlines.note: Archived (2024) version appends '[Update]'; no 2012 snapshot found.

headlines.text: Girls Around Me App: Not Today's Creepiest Stalker
Girls Around Me Dev: We Didn’t Do Anything Wrong [Statement]

what_happened.text: An iPhone app showed women who had checked in on Foursquare at nearby venues and pulled their public Facebook profiles and photos. Cult of Mac's report on 30 March 2012 drew wide coverage. The app had been downloaded more than 70,000 times, according to Dark Reading.

outcome_detail.text: Foursquare cut off the app's API access, citing its policy against aggregating information across venues, and the developer withdrew the app from the App Store. Facebook said it was investigating.

responses.summary: Said the app only let users browse nearby venues, 'as if you passed by and looked in the window', and showed no data users had not already shared.

sources.label: Cult of Mac on why Foursquare cut the app off

cases.title: Microsoft patent routes pedestrians around 'unsafe' neighborhoods

headlines.text: New Microsoft patent: Walking directions that avoid crime-ridden neighborhoods
Microsoft "avoid ghetto" patent sparks controversy
Microsoft Patents "Avoid Ghetto" Feature for GPS Devices

what_happened.text: Microsoft was granted US Patent 8,090,532, 'Pedestrian route production' (filed 2007), which describes walking directions that route around neighborhoods whose violent-crime statistics exceed a threshold, as well as around bad weather. Press coverage labeled it an 'avoid ghetto' feature; that phrase does not appear in the patent.

outcome_detail.text: Microsoft declined to comment. The patent stood. It is unclear whether the technique was ever deployed in Bing Maps.

responses.summary: Declined to comment to CBS Seattle.

cases.title: 'We kill people based on metadata'

headlines.text: Ex-NSA Chief: ‘We Kill People Based on Metadata’
U.S. Government Designated Prominent Al Jazeera Journalist as "Member of Al Qaeda"
The NSA’s SKYNET program may be killing thousands of innocent people

what_happened.text: Former NSA and CIA director Michael Hayden said in 2014 that 'we kill people based on metadata.' Snowden documents published by The Intercept in 2015 described SKYNET, a program that applied machine learning to the mobile phone metadata of about 55 million people in Pakistan to score their likelihood of being couriers for al Qaeda; one slide labeled Al Jazeera's Islamabad bureau chief a member of al Qaeda. A 2016 analysis by statistician Patrick Ball criticized the method as unsound.

outcome_detail.text: No public change to metadata-based targeting was announced. The NSA did not publicly address the critiques of SKYNET.

responses.summary: Denied membership in al Qaeda or the Muslim Brotherhood; said his contacts were normal journalism.

book_refs.note: Data Power ch. 1 (drone strikes on phone metadata; Scahill 2015)

cases.title: Uber executive tracks a journalist with 'God View'

headlines.text: Uber Battles Privacy Concerns Over 'God View' Tool
What Is Uber Really Doing With Your Data?
Uber is investigating its top New York exec for 'God View' privacy invasion

what_happened.text: BuzzFeed News reported that Uber's New York general manager, Josh Mohrer, told reporter Johana Bhuiyan he had been tracking her ride to an interview, using an internal tool employees called 'God View' that showed the real-time locations of cars and riders. Former employees said corporate staff had broad access to it.

outcome_detail.text: Uber said it disciplined Mohrer. In January 2016 Uber paid $20,000 to the New York Attorney General and agreed to encrypt location data. In 2017 it settled FTC charges about employee access to customer data, agreeing to 20 years of privacy audits without admitting wrongdoing.

responses.summary: Told NBC News that access to data is permitted only for legitimate business purposes and that violations lead to disciplinary action.

sources.label: CNBC on the FTC settlement, Aug 2017

cases.title: 'Anonymized' NYC taxi data reveals drivers and passengers

headlines.text: Poorly anonymized logs reveal NYC cab drivers’ detailed whereabouts
Improperly anonymized taxi logs reveal drivers’ identity, movements
Deanonymizing Taxi Passenger and Fare Data

what_happened.text: Chris Whong obtained 2013 trip records for about 173 million New York City taxi rides through a freedom-of-information request and published them. The medallion and license numbers had been hashed with MD5, and Vijay Pandurangan reversed them in under two hours. Researcher Anthony Tockar then matched rides to paparazzi photos of celebrities, and showed how the data could reveal the home addresses of regular visitors to a strip club.

outcome_detail.text: No public response from the Taxi and Limousine Commission was found.

sources.label: Gotham Gazette on the TLC and FOIL

cases.title: Public running-app routes mapped city by city

what_happened.text: Data visualizer Nathan Yau, building on work by Nikita Barsukov, scraped public RunKeeper routes and mapped where people run in major US cities. Precedent-only entry; not played as a card.

cases.title: Homelessness outreach data used to locate and deport EU rough sleepers

headlines.text: Home Office used charity data map to deport rough sleepers
Liberty exposes secret data-sharing deal between Greater London Authority and Home Office to deport rough sleepers
Charity may have shared rough sleepers' data without consent, watchdog finds

what_happened.text: Freedom-of-information requests by Liberty showed that Home Office immigration enforcement had access, from September 2016 to February 2017, to an interactive map built by the Greater London Authority from CHAIN, the London rough-sleeper database that charity outreach workers populate with details including nationality and regular sleeping locations. The Home Office was then detaining and removing EU nationals for sleeping rough.

outcome_detail.text: On 14 December 2017 the High Court (R (Gureckis) v SSHD [2017] EWHC 3298 (Admin)) ruled the Home Office policy of removing EU nationals for rough sleeping unlawful. The ruling concerned the removal policy, not the data sharing itself. The claimants were supported by the Public Interest Law Unit at Lambeth Law Centre and North East London Migrant Action. The Home Office said it stopped such operations after the ruling. In 2018 the ICO found St Mungo's had likely shared data without consent but had a public-interest defence.

responses.summary: Said it did not send CHAIN data to the Home Office, which instead had access to an online tool showing mapped CHAIN data.

sources.label: Corporate Watch on the court victory

book_refs.note: Data Power intro and ch. 1; Dalton et al. 2020

cases.title: Strava's Global Heatmap reveals military bases

headlines.text: Fitness tracking app Strava gives away location of secret US army bases
U.S. soldiers are revealing sensitive and dangerous information by jogging
Fitness app data is revealing military bases to enemy fighters

what_happened.text: Strava published a Global Heatmap in November 2017 built from about a billion uploaded activities. On 27 January 2018 analyst Nathan Ruser posted that it made US bases 'clearly identifiable and mappable', and others found bases and patrol routes in Afghanistan, Syria and elsewhere, where nearly all Strava users were military personnel.

outcome_detail.text: In March 2018 Strava limited street-level detail to logged-in users, required several athletes before low-traffic routes showed heat, and moved to monthly refreshes that drop data set to private. In August 2018 the Pentagon barred deployed personnel from using geolocation features in operational areas.

responses.summary: Said the map excluded activities marked private and user-defined privacy zones, and that it would work with military and government officials on sensitive areas.

book_refs.note: Data Power intro and ch. 1, Fig. 1.4

cases.title: Cambridge Analytica harvested Facebook profiles

headlines.text: Revealed: 50 million Facebook profiles harvested for Cambridge Analytica in major data breach
How Trump Consultants Exploited the Facebook Data of Millions

what_happened.text: The Observer and The New York Times reported, based on whistleblower Christopher Wylie, that Cambridge Analytica had obtained data on tens of millions of Facebook users through a personality-quiz app built by researcher Aleksandr Kogan, and used it to profile US voters. Facebook later put the number of affected users at up to 87 million.

outcome_detail.text: Cambridge Analytica shut down in May 2018. In July 2019 the FTC fined Facebook $5 billion and imposed new privacy restrictions.

responses.summary: Called the episode a breach of trust and said Facebook would audit apps that had accessed large amounts of data before it tightened its rules in 2014, and ban those that broke them.

cases.title: Polar Flow reveals home addresses of soldiers and spies

headlines.text: Fitness app Polar Flow reveals home addresses of soldiers, spies
Another fitness app reveals data that can be used to identify soldiers and spies
Polar fitness app broadcasted sensitive data of intelligence and military personnel

what_happened.text: Bellingcat and De Correspondent showed that Polar's public Explore map let anyone view all of a user's workouts on one map, revealing where people likely lived. They identified 6,460 users of 69 nationalities who exercised at about 200 sensitive sites, including military bases and intelligence agencies. An oversight meant some private profiles were also exposed.

outcome_detail.text: Polar temporarily suspended its Explore feature.

cases.title: Google keeps tracking location with Location History off

headlines.text: AP Exclusive: Google tracks your movements, like it or not
Google still tracks your location even when you turn off Location History
40 States Settle Google Location-Tracking Charges For $392M

what_happened.text: An Associated Press investigation, confirmed by Princeton researchers, found that many Google services on Android and iPhone stored timestamped location data even when users had turned off 'Location History', for example when opening Google Maps or running some searches. Google's help page had said that with Location History off, the places you go are no longer stored.

outcome_detail.text: Google changed its help-page wording. In November 2022 it agreed to pay $391.5 million to 40 states, which the attorneys general called the largest multistate privacy settlement in US history.

responses.summary: A spokesperson told the AP that it provides clear descriptions of its location tools and controls that let people turn them on or off.

cases.title: Apps sell precise location data to dozens of companies

headlines.text: Your Apps Know Where You Were Last Night, and They’re Not Keeping It Secret

what_happened.text: A New York Times investigation found at least 75 companies receiving precise location data from apps, some claiming to track up to 200 million US devices. Reporters analyzed a database of more than a million phones in the New York area, updated in some cases more than 14,000 times a day, and identified individuals in it who agreed to be named. App permission prompts often did not say the data would be sold.

outcome_detail.text: No regulatory action directly followed the investigation.

sources.label: SPJ awards entry for the investigation

cases.title: Bounty hunters buy real-time phone locations from carriers' data

headlines.text: I Gave a Bounty Hunter $300. Then He Located Our Phone
headlines.note: Page metadata title differs: 'T-Mobile, Sprint, and AT&T Are Selling Customers' Real-Time Location Data, And It's Falling Into the Wrong Hands'.

headlines.text: FCC seeks $200M in total fines against top wireless carriers

what_happened.text: Motherboard paid a bounty hunter $300 to locate a T-Mobile phone, which he did using real-time location data that the carrier had made available through data aggregators such as LocationSmart and Zumigo, which resold it.

outcome_detail.text: The carriers said they had ended or would end their aggregator programs. The FCC proposed about $209 million in fines in 2020 and finalized about $200 million in April 2024. In April 2025 the Fifth Circuit vacated AT&T's $57 million fine on jury-trial grounds; the government asked the Supreme Court to review amid conflicting rulings in other circuits.

responses.summary: Said it ended its location-aggregator program in February 2019 and would dispute the fine.

sources.label: Sen. Wyden on the FCC fines
Benton Institute on the Fifth Circuit ruling

cases.title: Immigration agencies buy app location data

headlines.text: Federal Agencies Use Cellphone Location Data for Immigration Enforcement
Trump's immigration enforcement agents use cellphone location data to track individuals for detention - WSJ
ICE, CBP Purchase Phone Location Data to Enforce Immigration Law: Report

what_happened.text: The Wall Street Journal reported that ICE and CBP had bought access to a commercial database of phone movements, drawn from ordinary apps such as games and weather apps, from Venntel, and used it for immigration and border enforcement. Because the data was bought rather than demanded from carriers, the government treated it as outside the warrant requirement of Carpenter v. United States (2018).

outcome_detail.text: The House Oversight Committee opened an investigation, and CBP renewed its Venntel contract. Later FOIA records showed DHS temporarily paused some Venntel-based projects over legal questions. In January 2025 the FTC finalized an order barring Venntel and its parent Gravy Analytics from selling sensitive location data except in limited circumstances.

responses.summary: A spokesman said the agency 'generally' did not use the data for deportation operations.

book_refs.note: Data Power ch. 2 (agencies purchasing data to circumvent warrants; Cox 2021)

cases.title: Reported: prayer app's location data reached US military contractors

headlines.text: How the U.S. Military Buys Location Data from Ordinary Apps
US military buys location data of popular Muslim apps: Report
‘Untrue’: Muslim Pro app denies selling user data to US military

what_happened.text: Motherboard reported two routes by which app location data reached the US military: Babel Street's Locate X product, bought by US Special Operations Command, and X-Mode, which collected location data through code embedded in apps and sold it to defense contractors. The most prominent app involved was Muslim Pro, a prayer and Quran app with more than 98 million downloads, which did not name X-Mode in its privacy policy. The military confirmed it used such data for overseas special operations.

outcome_detail.text: Muslim Pro ended its data partnerships. In December 2020 Apple and Google banned the X-Mode SDK from their app stores; a January 2021 report said X-Mode was still tracking users. In 2024 the FTC barred X-Mode and its successor Outlogic from selling sensitive location data (proposed January, finalized April).

responses.summary: Called the report 'untrue' and denied selling data to the US military, while ending its relationship with X-Mode. Motherboard's analysis found the app had sent location data to X-Mode.

sources.label: Vice on the app store bans

cases.title: Catholic news site uses commercial app data to report on a church official

headlines.text: Priest outed via Grindr app highlights rampant data tracking
Top U.S. Catholic church official resigns after cellphone data used to track him on Grindr and to gay bars
headlines.outlet: The Washington Post (via The Philadelphia Inquirer)

headlines.text: How a Catholic Priest Was Outed Using His Own Private Data

what_happened.text: Msgr. Jeffrey Burrill resigned as general secretary of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops ahead of a report by the Catholic outlet The Pillar, which said it had obtained 'commercially available records of app data signals' correlated to his phone showing near-daily Grindr use in parts of 2018 to 2020, including at gay bars. The Pillar did not name its data vendor or say whether it paid.

outcome_detail.text: No regulatory action followed. Burrill was later reassigned to a parish, and in July 2024 he sued Grindr over the alleged sale of his data.

cases.title: Family safety app sells families' precise locations

headlines.text: The Popular Family Safety App Life360 Is Selling Precise Location Data on Its Tens of Millions of Users
Life360 reportedly sells precise, identifiable location data

what_happened.text: The Markup reported, based on two former Life360 employees and two former employees of location-data brokers, that the family-tracking app (about 33 million users) sold precise location data, including on children, to roughly a dozen data brokers that resold it widely. The former employees said the company's anonymization did not prevent re-identification.

outcome_detail.text: Life360 said it would stop selling precise location data to most brokers, but would continue to sell precise data to Arity and aggregated data to Placer.ai.

responses.summary: CEO Chris Hulls said data sales are an important part of the business model that keeps core services free for most users.

cases.title: FTC sues a data broker over abortion-clinic visit data

headlines.text: FTC Sues ‘Massive’ Data Broker for Selling Location Info on Abortion Clinics
FTC sues data broker for selling sensitive information, including abortion clinic visits
The Fall of Roe Finally Prompts the FTC to Protect Our Location Data

what_happened.text: Two months after the Dobbs decision, the FTC sued Kochava, alleging that it sold precise location data tied to mobile advertising IDs that could reveal visits to abortion clinics, places of worship, domestic-violence shelters and other sensitive places. The FTC said Kochava had offered a free sample covering more than 61 million devices over one week.

outcome_detail.text: A federal judge dismissed the FTC's first complaint in 2023 and allowed it to amend. On 4 May 2026 the FTC announced a proposed order barring Kochava from selling sensitive location data without affirmative express consent.

responses.summary: Its data-marketplace manager told NBC News that 'real progress to improve data privacy for consumers will not be reached through flamboyant press releases and frivolous litigation.'

sources.label: White & Case on the 2026 settlement (JD Supra copy)

cases.title: Police buy access to app location data through Fog Reveal

headlines.text: Tech tool offers police ‘mass surveillance on a budget’
How an obscure cellphone tracking tool provides police ‘mass surveillance on a budget’

what_happened.text: A joint Associated Press and EFF investigation found that nearly two dozen US law enforcement agencies had contracts for Fog Reveal, a tool that searched hundreds of billions of location records from about 250 million devices, drawn from advertising IDs in apps, to build 'patterns of life', often without a warrant. A basic subscription allowed 100 searches a month.

outcome_detail.text: Members of Congress criticized the tool and some called for an FTC investigation. At least one city (Greensboro, NC) let its contract lapse. No ban or enforcement action was found.

responses.summary: Said it does not hold personal information and that search warrants are not required.

cases.title: Bluetooth trackers used to stalk women

headlines.text: I Used Apple AirTags, Tiles and a GPS Tracker to Watch My Husband’s Every Move
Police Records Show Women Are Being Stalked With Apple AirTags Across the Country

what_happened.text: Motherboard obtained 150 police reports mentioning AirTags from eight US departments over eight months; in 50, women reported being alerted that an AirTag they did not own was tracking them, and in 25 of those they suspected a specific man in their lives. A New York Times reporter's test found AirTags tracked well in cities, while Tile and a GPS tracker gave no warning at all.

outcome_detail.text: Apple updated its unwanted-tracking alerts in 2022. A class action was filed in December 2022. Apple and Google announced a cross-platform alert standard in May 2023; Android alerts arrived in 2023 and iOS 17.5 added alerts for other brands' trackers in May 2024.

sources.label: The Register on cross-platform alerts, May 2024

cases.title: Bodyguards' Strava runs reveal heads of state's whereabouts

headlines.text: Fitness app Strava gives away location of Biden, Trump and other leaders, French newspaper says
Merde! Macron's bodyguards reveal his location by sharing Strava data
Via Strava: Bodyguards make the whereabouts of heads of state public
Jogging app Strava reveals locations of heads of state
headlines.note: Kicker above headline: 'Macron, Biden and Putin affected'.

what_happened.text: Le Monde found 26 US Secret Service agents, 12 members of the French presidential security group and six members of Russia's FSO sharing workouts publicly on Strava, from which it could locate leaders including Biden, Harris, Trump, Macron and Putin. One example was a private 2021 weekend Macron spent in Honfleur that was not on his official schedule.

outcome_detail.text: Some bodyguards made their profiles private or deleted them. The Élysée said the risk was non-existent; the Secret Service said protection was not compromised and that it does not prohibit off-duty personal social media use.

responses.summary: Said it did not believe protection was compromised; staff cannot use personal devices on duty but are not barred from personal social media off duty.

cases.title: Hack of a location-data broker exposes data from thousands of apps

headlines.text: Candy Crush, Tinder, MyFitnessPal: See the Thousands of Apps Hijacked to Spy on Your Location
Hackers claim massive breach of company that tracks and sells Americans' location data

what_happened.text: Hackers claimed to have breached Gravy Analytics, parent of Venntel, which had sold app-derived location data to US agencies. Gravy's parent Unacast disclosed that its cloud storage had been accessed using a misappropriated access key. Leaked samples named thousands of apps, including games, dating and fitness apps, whose users' locations appeared to have been collected, largely through ad networks.

outcome_detail.text: The FTC had announced a proposed order against Gravy and Venntel on 3 December 2024, before the breach. It finalized the order on 14 January 2025, barring the companies from selling sensitive location data except in limited national-security and law-enforcement circumstances. The FTC said the companies processed over 17 billion signals a day from about a billion devices.

responses.summary: Disclosed unauthorized access to its AWS environment via a misappropriated access key.

cases.title: Reported: a sheriff's plate-camera search logged as 'had an abortion'

headlines.text: A Texas Cop Searched License Plate Cameras Nationwide for a Woman Who Got an Abortion
She Got an Abortion. So A Texas Cop Used 83,000 Cameras to Track Her Down.
Texas officer used Flock ALPR network to search for a woman suspected of abortion
headlines.note: Page metadata title differs: 'A Texas officer used Flock to track down a woman who got an abortion'.

what_happened.text: 404 Media reported that a Johnson County, Texas, deputy searched Flock's network of more than 83,000 license-plate cameras across 6,809 networks, including in states where abortion is legal, with the logged reason 'had an abortion, search for female.' EFF described the access as 'warrant-less'.

outcome_detail.text: Flock and the sheriff disputed the reporting. Records later reported by EFF include a detective's affidavit describing a death investigation opened after a report of an abortion. Several cities have since voted to end Flock contracts, citing a range of concerns.

responses.party: Johnson County Sheriff's Office and Flock Safety
responses.summary: The sheriff said the search was for a missing person whose safety the family feared for; Flock called media accounts 'false', 'misleading' and 'clickbait'.

cases.title: Women's dating-safety app leaks selfies and IDs, some with GPS

headlines.text: Tea, an app for women to anonymously talk about men they date, has been breached, user IDs exposed
The Tea app was intended to help women date safely. Then it got hacked
Tea app fallout worsens as leaked selfies used in rating site, online map

what_happened.text: Users of 4chan found an exposed storage system belonging to Tea, an app where women share information about men they date. It held about 72,000 images, including about 13,000 verification selfies and photo IDs, from users who joined before February 2024. Some images carried GPS metadata, and maps of affected women's locations circulated online.

outcome_detail.text: Tea said the vulnerability was fixed and new security protocols were in place. It said the leaked verification images had been retained to comply with law-enforcement guidance on cyberbullying.

responses.summary: Said a legacy data storage system was compromised, no emails or phone numbers were exposed, and the vulnerability was fixed.
